Aerobic bimetallic catalysis for oxy-alkynylation of
allenes†
Junjie Fan,
 ‡ Dongjie Zhang,
 ‡ Yaqi Shi, Chunling Fu and Shengming Ma
 *
Here we report a conceptual protocol to construct 4-alkynyl furan-2(5 H)-one derivatives e ﬃciently
through Rh(III)/Cu(I) co-catalyzed highly regioselective oxy-alkynylation of 2,3-allenoic acids with terminal
alkynes under mild aerobic conditions with atom economy. A wide variety of functional groups including
biologically active groups have been tolerated. The synthetic potentials have also been demonstrated and
the total syntheses of natural product appenolide A and its ( Z)-isomer have been achieved by applying this
protocol as the key step e ﬃciently. A mechanism has been proposed based on mechanistic studies.
Introduction
Alkynyl or ( Z)o r( E)-alkenyl-substituted cyclic structural units
are commonly observed in natural and/or biologically active
products. For example, aza- and oxa-cyclic structurals bearing
alkynyl or alkenyl exist in indole alkaloid P1, penaresin, anhy-
droanthramycin, rauvoloid D, chondriamide A, brevisyne A,
VVD-118313, aureonitol, asparo ﬃn A, cleviolide, appenolide A,
palauolide, Scutebarbatine A, pezizolide F, piterrione A, inono-
farnesane, and spicatanol, etc. (Scheme 1).
1 As we know,
Sonogashira coupling reactions of electrophilic organic halides
with terminal alkynes have been established as one of the
most e ﬃcient ways for the syntheses of substituted alkynes
(Scheme 2a).
2,3 We envisioned a concept of the coupling reac-
tion of cyclo alkenyl or alkyl metallic species in situ formed via
the cyclic nucleometalation of unsaturated hydrocarbons with
a nucleophilic functionality with terminal alkynes for the
eﬃcient synthesis of alkynyl-substituted cyclic skeleton
(Scheme 2b), which should be a platform reaction for the
selective synthesis of alkynyl or ( Z)o r( E)-alkenyl-substituted
cyclic compounds listed in Scheme 1. The key here is the
match of the reactivity of these two species, the regeneration of
the catalyst, Glaser –Hay coupling reaction of the terminal
alkynes applied, and the regioselectivity of the cyclization
reaction.
4,5 Here we wish to report the realization of such a
concept, i.e., Rh( III)/Cu(I) co-catalyzed highly selective oxy-alky-
nylation of 2,3-allenoic acids 6 with terminal alkynes applying
oxygen in air as the green oxidant for the e ﬃcient regeneration
of the catalytically active tri-valent rhodium species
(Scheme 2c).
Scheme 1 Natural and/or biologically active products containing β-C–
C triple or double bonds.

Results and discussion
Our e ﬀorts commenced with a model reaction of 2-propyl-2,3-
butadienoic acid 1a and tert-butyl pent-4-ynoate 2a. After
tedious optimization, the optimal reaction conditions have
been defined: the reaction of allenoic acid 1a (0.2 mmol) and
terminal alkyne 2a (1.3 equiv.) under the catalysis of
[Cp*RhCl2]2 (2.5 mol%) and CuI (15 mol%) with i-Pr 2NH (1.0
equiv.) as the base in a 1 : 1 mixture of DME (1,2-dimethoxy-
ethane)/toluene (0.2 M) under air atmosphere at 50 °C giving
4-alkynylfuran-2(5H)-one 3aa in 71% NMR yield (Table 1, entry
1). Meanwhile, the formation of Glaser –Hay coupling reaction
product diyne 2a′ was also observed.
7 Some other metal cata-
lysts, such as PdCl 2, Pd(PPh 3)2Cl2, Pd(PhCN) 2Cl2, Pd(OAc) 2,
[Cp*IrCl2]2, Cp*RuCl 2, Ni(OAc) 2·4H2O, and Cp*CoI 2(CO) were
surveyed, with no better results (entries 2 –9). Upon using the
single solvent of toluene or DME, the yield was slightly lower
(entries 10 and 11). Increasing or decreasing the loading of
terminal alkyne 2a failed to improve the yield (entries 12 and
13). Interestingly, the oxygen in air is necessary for this reac-
tion, and using the pure oxygen resulted in a much lower yield
(entries 14 and 15). Each of [Cp*RhCl
2]2, CuI, and i-Pr 2NH are
required (entries 16–18).
With the optimal conditions in hand, the scope of oxy-alky-
nylation of 2,3-allenoic acids 1 and terminal alkynes 2 was
then investigated (Table 2). The terminal alkynes with simple
1°-alkyl chains 2b–2d reacted with 2,3-allenoic acid 1a to
aﬀord corresponding products 3ab–3ad in decent yields. The
strained cyclopropyl-substituted acetylene also gave the
desired product 3ae. The alkynes bearing highly reactive func-
tional groups, such as tert-butoxycarbonyl group ( 2a), halide
(Cl and Br), hydroxy and protected hydroxy, all could be toler-
ated giving the corresponding 2-furan-5( H)-ones 3aa and 3af–
3ak in 60% –70% yields. Cyano and thiocyanato with remark-
able coordinating ability could also be tolerated to a ﬀord 3al
and 3am in excellent yields. Besides the alkyl alkynes, di ﬀerent
aryl-substituted acetylenes could also a ﬀord target products
3an and 3ao smoothly. Menthol ( 2p), steroid skeleton ( 2q and
2r), and ( S)-ibuprofen ( 2s) may all be incorporated to a ﬀord
the related products 3ap∼(S)-3as in excellent yields.
Then di ﬀerently substituted 2,3-allenoic acids were further
investigated with some terminal alkynes: the R 1 of allenoic
acids may be methyl, phenylethyl, chloropropyl, and alkox-
yalkyl groups etc. producing 3ba–3ea. In addition, the C –C
double and triple bonds remained untouched a ﬀording 3fa
and 3ga. Synthetically versatile functionalities such as F, Cl,
Br, OMe, and CF
3 may be installed on the benzyl group
aﬀording 3ha–3ma in moderate yields. The structure of the
products has further been confirmed by the X-ray di ﬀraction
study on the single crystal of 3ma. With trisubstituted allenoic
acids, the yields are lower, indicating an obvious steric e ﬀect
(3nh–3ph). The in situ formed 5-phenylfuran-2(5 H)-one from
the reaction of 1p with 2b was further oxidized a ﬀording
γ-hydroxylated product 5 by air.8

In order to explore the synthetic potentials of this protocol,
a gram-scale reaction has been conducted under the standard
conditions a ﬀording 3ai in 71% yield. The hydroxy group in
3ai could be oxidized in dichloroethane to produce the alde-
hyde 6 in air by using Fe(NO 3)3·9H2O, 4-OH-TEMPO, and NaCl
as the catalysts. 9 CuCl-catalyzed hydroboration 10 of 3ai pro-
duced an alkenyl borate ( E)-7 in 75% NMR yield, which under-
went cross-coupling with iodobenzene catalyzed by Pd(PPh 3)4
to yield product ( E)-8 in 52% yield (39% from 3ai to ( E)-8).11
Appenolide A, isolated from liquid cultures of the coprophi-
lous fungus Podospora appendiculata , exhibited both antibac-
terial and antifungal activities. 1m Alkylation of ethyl acetoace-
tate 9 with 6-iodo-1-hexyne 10 aﬀorded terminal alkyne 11 in
95% yield. Subsequent decarboxylation a ﬀorded terminal
alkynyl methyl ketone 2t in 91% yield. Its reaction with
2-methyl-2,3-butadienoic acid 1b under the standard con-
ditions a ﬀorded 3bt in 51% yield. Cp*Ru(CH 3CN)2PF6-cata-
lyzed trans-hydrosilylation12 and the desilylation 13 aﬀorded
appenolide A in 88% combined yield for the last two steps
while ( Z)-isomer of appenolide A was provided through cis-
hydrogenation catalyzed by Lindlar catalyst in 84% yield
(Scheme 3).
To clarify the mechanism, a series of control reactions were
conducted: when allenoic acid 1a was stirred under the stan-
dard conditions in the absence of a terminal alkyne, 4% NMR
yield of β-iodofuran-2(5H)-one 4 was detected (Scheme 4,
eqn (1)). However, using CuBr instead of CuI, the corres-
ponding bromide 12 was not formed (eqn (2)). Using 4 instead
of 2,3- allenoic acid 1a failed to a ﬀord the target product 3ac
under the standard conditions (eqn (3)), suggesting that 4 was
not the intermediate for this transformation.
14 When 1.0
equiv. of copper( I) butylacetylenide was added instead of term-
inal alkynes, target product 3ab was formed in 27% NMR yield
(eqn (4)). In addition, when 15 mol% of copper( I) butylacetyle-
nide was applied instead of CuI in the presence of terminal
alkyne containing OTHP group 2j, the reaction a ﬀorded 3aj in
61% yield with the product 3ab with the alkynyl from copper( I)
butylacetylenide in 3% yield (eqn (5)), demonstrating that
alkynyl copper was the intermediate.
On the basis of these experimental data, a mechanism was
proposed as shown in Scheme 5. In path A, the terminal
alkyne would be converted to the alkynyl copper Int I in the
presence of base and copper( I). After transmetallation between
Int I and the rhodium( III) catalyst, alkynyl rhodium( III) Int II ,
which would trigger the nucleorhodation 15 of 2,3-allenoic acid
1 to a ﬀord Int IV via the coordination complex Int III .
Reductive elimination would a ﬀord the product 3 and
rhodium(I) species, which would be oxidized back to the cata-
lytically active rhodium( III) species to furnish the catalytic cycle
with the oxygen from air as the green oxidant. 16 Alternatively,
the nucleorhodation may take place firstly to a ﬀord furan-2
(5H)-one-4-yl rhodium intermediate Int VI . Transmetallation
between Int VI and Int I would also a ﬀord the same intermedi-
ate Int IV (Path B). There is still an alternative pathway, which

could not be excluded (Path C): 17 the 2,3-allenoic acid 1 may

product 3 and rhodium(I) species.
Conclusions
In conclusion, we have developed an e ﬃcient Rh( III)/Cu(I) co-
catalyzed regioselectivity-defined cyclic oxy-alkynylation of 2,3-
allenoic acids with terminal alkynes, a ﬀording 4-alkynylfuran-
2(5H)-one derivatives. The synthetic potentials have also been
demonstrated. Both antifungal and antibacterial natural
product, appenolide A and its Z-isomer have been synthesized
highly stereoselectively by using this reaction as the key step. A
Rh(III)/Rh(I) catalytic cycle has been proposed for the reaction.
